title: This Factory Let Workers Choose Their Hours—and It Was a Game Changer!
summary: Imagine if you could decide when to go to work—and for how long. That's exactly what's happening at a factory in LaFayette, Georgia. The Roper Corporation, which makes ovens and stoves, was in big trouble during the pandemic. People were buying tons of appliances because they were stuck at home cooking. But the factory didn't have enough workers. Some days, they were short by hundreds of people! So the bosses tried something unusual: flexible shifts. Instead of requiring everyone to work 40 hours a week, they let workers sign up for four-hour shifts using an app called MyWorkChoice. Ruth Ransom, a 68-year-old grandma, loves it. She only wanted to work a couple of days a week to get out of the house. Now she picks shifts that fit her life. About 450 flexible workers do this every week, working an average of 24 hours. The idea was so successful that the company expanded the plant, adding 600 new jobs. It turns out giving workers more choice can be a win for everyone.
why_it_matters: When companies give workers the choice to pick their hours, families like yours can spend more time together and parents can manage work and home better.

background_read: Factory jobs usually have the same shifts every day, but that made it hard to find enough workers when demand shot up.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, many people stayed home and cooked more, so appliance sales skyrocketed.
That’s when the Roper Corporation in LaFayette, Georgia (a small town) tried flexible shifts for the first time.
Article_Structure: WHO: The Roper Corporation, its workers (including 68-year-old Ruth Ransom).
WHAT: The factory started letting workers sign up for flexible 4-hour shifts using an app.
WHY: The factory lacked enough workers to meet high demand for appliances during the pandemic.

perspectives.description: Workers love being able to fit jobs around their lives, especially older people or those with family duties.
Some bosses were worried that flexible shifts would cause chaos, but the success of the idea showed it really works.
